solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Border enforcement chief, in case London's not as bad as Farage & co claim

definitions.text: London's not as bad as Farage & co claim

indicators.note: in places the border letters inside the case word

parts.note: a crate is a packing case
a rim is a border

indicators.note: chief means the head or first letter of the following word

parts.note: first letter E

explanation.surface: The border enforcement boss argues London is safer than Farage and his allies claim.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic sentence: London's figure for offences is not as bad as Farage and Reform claim.
explanation.definitionFit: Politicians argue over the level of offending in the capital, the statistic measured as incidents per head.

clue.text: Pence temporarily given immunity at last, which is more than sufficient

definitions.note: The answer is a noun of quantity and the definition an adjectival phrase: it is pointing at the everyday use in which 'that is plenty' says there is more there than the job needs.

parts.note: p is the coin on every British price tag
something handed over for a while and wanted back has been lent

indicators.note: What comes at last in a word is the letter it finishes on, so one letter is taken from the end of the word before it.

parts.note: the letter that word ends on

explanation.surface: Mike Pence handed immunity for the time being, and a verdict on how generous that is.
explanation.walkthrough: Pence is the vice-president in the sentence and small change in the wordplay, which is the whole of the misdirection. Immunity is a long word supplying a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty is having more of something than you need, which is what more than sufficient says in the formal register.

clue.text: Funeral introduces new form of detention

indicators.note: To introduce something is to bring it in, so the letter named next goes inside the word standing before it.

parts.note: an interment is a burial, the part of a funeral that puts the body in the ground
n is the standard short form of new

explanation.surface: A burial service ushering in some freshly invented way of locking people up.
explanation.walkthrough: Two long words that differ by one letter sit either side of the parse, which is what lets the surface talk about funerals and prisons in the same breath. New is an adjective in the sentence and a single letter in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Internment is holding people without charge or trial, usually in wartime, which is one recognised form of detention.

clue.text: Far-right broadcaster producing book soon about "Nationalism chiefly"

indicators.note: about means the soon word goes around the other letter

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon

indicators.note: chiefly means taking the first letter of the word

parts.note: first letter N

explanation.surface: A hard-right podcaster puts out a book soon about nationalism.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Bannon is the American far-right strategist who hosts the War Room podcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Bannon, former Trump adviser, hosts a nationalist show on air and online.

clue.text: Arse-over-tip police force's making arrest

definitions.note: arrest as a verb, to stop or check, which matches the verb stem

indicators.note: arse over tip is British slang for head over heels, upside down, so the word is turned over and read backwards

parts.note: the Met is the Metropolitan Police, London's force; with the 's it gives METS

explanation.surface: The London police tumble over themselves while detaining a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrest' looks like a police word but here means halt, as in arresting a decline; to stem the flow is the same sense. The Met is London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem something, such as bleeding or a tide, is to stop or check it, which is to arrest it.

clue.text: Swinger's nude balls hidden by fruit

indicators.note: hidden by means covered by, so the jumbled letters go inside the fruit

parts.note: a plum is a fruit

indicators.note: to balls something up is British slang for making a mess of it, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A naked partygoer's private parts are covered up by a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balls' rearranges NUDE to ENDU, and 'hidden by' tucks that inside PLUM after the P. 'Swinger' suggests a wife-swapper, but it is anything that swings.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendulum is a weight hung so that it swings to and fro, as in a clock, so it is a literal swinger.

clue.text: Chant "Trump's almost content"

indicators.note: The content of something is what sits inside it, so a run of letters within the words quoted is what is wanted.

parts.note: five letters running straight on through those two words, the apostrophe stepped over as crossword spelling allows

explanation.surface: Trump declared to be very nearly satisfied with something.
explanation.walkthrough: Almost sits exactly where an instruction to dock a word of its last letter would sit, and supplies three of the letters instead. The apostrophe in the middle of the run is what makes it hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalm is one of the Psalter's sacred songs, delivered in church by chanting rather than singing, so chant names it by how it is performed.

clue.text: Tempting to switch sides, being a monarch

definitions.note: a participle phrase: ruling means reigning, as a monarch does

indicators.note: the sides are left and right, so the letters for left and right trade places in the tempting word

parts.note: luring means tempting

explanation.surface: A politician is tempted to defect, as if that were the way to reign.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right; swapping them in LURING turns it into RULING.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruling means reigning or holding sovereign power, which is what being a monarch is.

clue.text: Imprudent time to reduce the stage appearances

parts.note: t is the standard short form of time
cutting down how often you go on stage is acting less, and the two words run together

explanation.surface: Telling a performer it is time they were seen on stage rather less often.
explanation.walkthrough: The long chunk is a plain instruction — act less — dressed as a comment on a fading career, and only the join between its two words does any hiding. Time gives up its usual single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody tactless says the thing better left unsaid, which is imprudent in the sense of lacking judgement rather than lacking caution.

clue.text: "Led astray in one of Epstein's homes? Not I" — ex-peer

indicators.note: in means inside, so the scrambled letters go within the shortened house
not I means leave out the letter I

parts.note: Jeffrey Epstein owned a mansion in Manhattan, among other grand houses

indicators.note: gone astray means wandered off course, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A former lord protests he was not the one led astray at a Jeffrey Epstein residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not I' drops I from MANSION to leave MANSON, and 'astray' rearranges LED to DEL, which goes 'in' it. Peter Mandelson lost his peerage over his links to Epstein.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mandelson, the Labour grandee, sat in the House of Lords as a life baron, so he is a former member of the peerage.

clue.text: They come in twos, bashes

definitions.note: The first definition is a sentence about the things rather than a name for them, identifying them by the pair they are always sold and worn in.
definitions.meaning: one goes on each foot, and shops sell them by the pair
as a noun, bashes are hard blows with the fist

explanation.walkthrough: Bashes reads as parties on the way past and has to be taken as thumps. A comma is the only thing marking the seam between two definitions, which is what makes the first half read as scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Socks are worn and sold in pairs, and a sock is also a heavy blow, so both halves land on the same plural.

clue.text: Head of Dept. involved in, say, Barbie award

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it starts with, here the shortened word that follows.
Say marks what follows as one example of a wider thing, so it is the general word that the letters spell.

parts.note: a barbie is Australian for a barbecue, which is one way of feeding people

indicators.note: Something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so that letter sits within the word named next.

parts.note: the opening letter of the shortened word

explanation.surface: A departmental boss mixed up in some prize given to a Barbie doll.
explanation.walkthrough: Barbie is the doll in the sentence and the Australian barbecue in the wordplay, with say quietly promoting it to the general word. The full stop after Dept. belongs to the abbreviation, not to the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A medal is the struck disc pinned on for bravery or for winning, which is an award in the most literal sense of the word.

clue.text: Shaft our national leaders for fake material

parts.note: a shaft of sunlight is a ray of it

indicators.note: The leaders of words are the letters standing at their front, one taken from each.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of those two words

explanation.surface: Doing the country's leaders over in exchange for something counterfeit.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaft is the verb of the sentence, to do somebody down, and a noun of light in the parse. Our national leaders sounds like politicians and is two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is the cellulose fibre sold for a century as artificial silk, so fake material names it by the cloth it stands in for.

clue.text: Mocking Clegg not quite fitting into lacy creation

indicators.note: fitting into means going inside, so the shortened name sits within the rearranged letters
a creation is a fashioned garment, so the letters are refashioned into a new order
not quite means falling a little short, so the last letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: Nick Clegg is the former Liberal Democrat leader and UK deputy prime minister

explanation.surface: Someone makes fun of Nick Clegg squeezing into a frilly outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creation' rearranges LACY to CYAL, and 'not quite' trims NICK to NIC, which goes 'fitting into' it after CY.
explanation.definitionFit: Cynical in the sense of sneering and scornful of others' motives, which is close to mocking or derisive.

clue.text: And Corbyn, pissed, stifles half-laugh — bastard's gone for a drink

indicators.note: to stifle a laugh is to smother it, so the rearranged letters close round it
pissed means drunk, so the remaining letters stagger into a new order
gone means taken away, so the bastard's letter is removed from the fodder

parts.note: B is the euphemistic abbreviation for bastard, as in 'B-word'
ha is half of ha-ha, a laugh

explanation.surface: A satirical scene: Jeremy Corbyn, drunk, smothers a giggle, and some bastard has left to get a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: AND CORBYN without its B ('bastard's gone') is ANDCORYN; 'pissed' rearranges it to C..ARDONNAY, which 'stifles' HA. Pissed is British slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Chardonnay is a popular white wine, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Announcer POTUS put off ("No depth!")

parts.note: POTUS is the President of the United States, and the present holder is the paper's favourite subject

indicators.note: No says the thing it names is absent, so that letter is missing from the word standing before it.

parts.note: to put somebody off doing something is to deter them
d is the short form a plan or a chart uses for depth

explanation.surface: The president dismissing something as having no depth to it whatever.
explanation.walkthrough: No depth is a verdict in the sentence and an instruction in the parse, and the letter it removes is the one a drawing writes for depth. A trumpeter is the herald who sounds the fanfare when somebody grand arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: A trumpeter blows the fanfare that announces an arrival, so announcer names the man by the job rather than by his instrument.

clue.text: Semi-nude cast going round some place east

indicators.note: going round means the toss word surrounds the other letters

parts.note: to cast is to toss
PL, part of place, is its usual abbreviation
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A half-dressed cast tours some place in the east.
explanation.definitionFit: Topless means bare above the waist, so the person is partly unclothed.

clue.text: View of old Republican stuffing a foreign country

indicators.note: To stuff something into a thing is to cram it inside, so those letters sit in the middle of the word named next.

parts.note: Panama is the Central American republic of the canal, foreign from a British desk
o is the standard short form of old
r is how the American party is shortened beside a result

explanation.surface: An elderly Republican cramming himself into a small foreign republic.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is the BBC's long-running current-affairs programme, so view of can be heard as a broadcast; the answer wants the plain word for a wide prospect. The country is named nowhere and has to be guessed from its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is the whole sweep of country visible from a high point, which is view taken at its widest.

clue.text: Many jerks ruin the country!

indicators.note: jerks means sudden jolts, so the letters are jolted into a new order

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or ruin

explanation.surface: An outburst that a lot of idiots are wrecking the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jerks' looks like a noun for fools but is a verb, jolting MANY into MYAN, followed by MAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Myanmar, formerly Burma, is a nation in South-East Asia.

clue.text: Precocious girl turns up without changing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pert, precocious young girl
second meaning: a palindrome, which in a down answer reads the same when turned to run bottom to top

explanation.surface: A forward young girl shows up looking exactly the same as before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns up' looks like 'arrives', but in a down clue it means reversing; the answer reads the same either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Madam is the British term for a cheeky, self-assured little girl who acts older than her years.

clue.text: "NO WAY IT'S MY IMMIGRATION TEAM!" Donald at first remarked

parts.note: no way is a flat refusal, which is what the little negative does in three letters
ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the American agency running the deportation raids

indicators.note: What comes at first is the opening letter of the name standing before it.

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Trump bellowing that the squad on the news has nothing to do with him.
explanation.walkthrough: The shouting capitals are surface noise and the agency's initials are standing in them in plain sight. Remarked is the definition in its older sense of taking note rather than of saying anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To remark something, in the sense the word keeps in writing, is to take note of it, which is what noticed says in the plainer register.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Delusion of Democrat: to have a following of many papers

indicators.note: Something with a following has things coming along behind it, so the letters named next take their place after the first one.

parts.note: d is how the American party is shortened beside a candidate's name
a ream is five hundred sheets of paper

explanation.surface: A Democrat fantasising about having the whole press behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: Papers are newspapers in the sentence and sheets in the parse, with many turning them into the stationer's quantity. Delusion picks the unkind one of the answer's two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream in the sense of a fond belief with nothing behind it is a delusion, which is the harsh word for the same thing.

clue.text: Injured arse (raised pimple) — I must go for a substitute

indicators.note: an injured part is damaged and out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
something that must go is removed, so the letter I is taken out
in a down answer, raising a word lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a zit is slang for a pimple

explanation.surface: A bruised backside with a raised spot, and someone needs a stand-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injured' rearranges ARSE to ERSA; 'raised' turns ZIT to TIZ, from which 'I must go' leaves TZ.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz, from German, is also a noun in dictionaries such as Chambers: an inferior imitation used in place of the real thing.

clue.text: Elected Conservative put on tights?

indicators.note: In a down entry what is put on something sits above it, so that letter goes in front of the rest.

parts.note: c is the short form printed beside the party on a ballot paper
hose is the old collective word for stockings and tights

explanation.surface: A Tory who got into parliament and then pulled on a pair of tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Elected Conservative wants to be one phrase naming an MP, and the tense settles it: the definition is the past of a verb. The question mark concedes that tights are only one kind of hose.
explanation.definitionFit: To choose is to elect in the sense of settling on one option — the committee elected to wait — and both words are in the past tense.

clue.text: Group of wives shoot male

parts.note: to shoot off somewhere is to hare off, going flat out
m is the standard short form of male

explanation.surface: A pack of wives taking aim at some man.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoot is a verb of speed here rather than of guns, and the animal it names is doing the running. The wives at the front are the definition, so no shooting survives into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the body of wives and concubines kept by one man, so group of wives names them collectively.

clue.text: (& 21ac.) Nick, coach has itch to back a leader on Trump's hate list

definitions.text: a leader on Trump's hate list

indicators.note: has means holds alongside, so the next piece is added on

parts.note: a nick is a small cut or notch, a mark
a car is a railway coach or carriage

indicators.note: to back something is to send it in reverse, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a yen is an itch or craving

explanation.surface: A bus driver with an urge supports a politician whom Donald Trump detests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to back' turns YEN into NEY. Mark Carney, Canada's prime minister, has clashed with Trump over tariffs and his talk of annexing Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Carney became Canada's prime minister in 2025 and is a frequent target of Donald Trump's hostility.

clue.text: Recall miners messing with ICE

indicators.note: Something messed about with does not come out as it went in, so the letters change order.

parts.note: six of the nine letters, waiting to be reordered
the American immigration agency, whose three letters join the pile

explanation.surface: Miners squaring up to the immigration enforcers.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are the only sign that those three letters are raw material and not frozen water. Recall is a verb here, which is what stops it being the noun a manufacturer issues.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to dwell fondly on times past, which is recall in its remembering sense rather than its summoning-back one.

clue.text: Those commonly held back by tosser playing for the county

indicators.note: held by means gripped inside, so the reversed piece goes within the jumbled letters
with held, by names the piece that does the holding
playing means at play, so the letters are moved about
back means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: 'em is the common, casual spoken form of them, meaning those

explanation.surface: An idiot plays sport for his county and keeps a few people back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns EM into ME; 'playing' rearranges TOSSER to SORSET, and 'held by' puts ME within that after SO. Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is a county in south-west England, famous for its cider and its county cricket team.

clue.text: Shed attached to the French chateau

parts.note: a snake sheds its skin, which is to cast it
the French for the, in its masculine form

explanation.surface: A garden shed tacked onto a French country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Shed is a verb here and not the thing at the bottom of the garden, with casting a skin the sense wanted. A chateau is the French country seat, often fortified and moated.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is the French castle or grand country seat, so the French word names the English building type outright.
